quotes.text: If I have to choose between a day when my mental illness was making me feel terrible, and a day when my mental illness was making me feel terrible, but I wrote a song, I'd take the second one.

I'd decided that I had completely lost touch with reality—and that I needed help. This was not depression. This was not workaholism. I have a fairly severe mental illness that makes it hard to do my job—in fact, makes me totally ill suited for my job. I have a form of dissociative disorder that makes the world seem like it's not real, as if things aren't taking place. It's hard to explain, but you feel untethered. And because nothing seems real, it's hard to connect with the world or the people in it because they're not there. You're not there. That's why I rarely saw my family back then: It's hard to care when everything feels as if it's taking place in your imagination. And if you're distant with people, especially women you're romantically involved with, they eventually leave. What makes my case even worse is that every night I go out on stage and have this incredible emotional connection between me, the band, and the audience. Then, just like that, it's over. Not really. It was just a story that started to gel about a couple kids. I guess I had just watched Ken Burns' Jack Johnson documentary. Another thing that happened is Lou Reed died when I was probably about three-quarters of the way through writing it. I'm not sure how big of an influence that was, but it was part of it. The song was about a period that's fascinating because of guys like Lou Reed — the early '70s and the late '60s with the Velvet Underground and Andy Warhol in New York.

Bill Fishman did a great job. A fantastic job. I mean, I usually don't like videos very much because you work very hard on a song to make it have a certain emotional weight and then a guy coming in to make a video, he's not coming at it from the same place. So your whole record is something you've put all this focus into and then you choose to represent it with somebody else's take on it. I never think it's a very good idea. But I talked to him from the beginning about approaching it like a film and not a music video. I said, "I don't want to be in it. Let's make it a film and express it."

Oh, yeah. The reason we made "Underwater Sunshine" wasn't that I wasn't writing. I was writing for a play. And I didn't want to write for two different things at once and have to choose, "Well, this song goes here. This song goes there." It just seemed confusing. And the truth is, "Underwater Sunshine" wasn't that different a process from any other record. We were just collaborating with people who weren't in the room. You learn a lot. And it's funny because the band got hugely better live after we made "Underwater Sunshine." I've said this a million times, but when you make a record like that, it makes you realize how much of a weakness it is to spend your whole career only recording one person's songs. Even in this case when the one person is me. There's so much more out there as a musician to be interested in. And I thought that record really helped open us to a lot of that.

And because of the play, for the first time, I was writing for other voices than my own. I was writing for a different range of men's voices. Women's voices. Writing for characters that weren't me. And I found that really liberating. So I think the combination of those two things really informs this record.

I really love theater. Living in New York, it's something I've loved all my life. And I got interested in working on it with a Broadway playwright. We're probably never going to finish it because we're both so busy. I get a free minute, and he's directing a movie. Or he's got a new play going on. He gets a free minute, and I'm in the studio making a record or going out on tour. Having those schedules, we've been doing it together for seven years but we barely get any time to work on it.

I think maybe the realization that I could do it differently? The last couple years of touring, following "Underwater Sunshine," were so good for us. The band has always been good live, but we took this huge leap. We spent these two years just crushing it on the road. And at that point, it's like your band is such a finely tuned instrument, you want to make a record.

Well, we've always collaborated. This was a little more formal, though. I asked some of the guys to come stay at my house so we kind of camped out for a week every month after the tour ended last summer. We wrote all this stuff in the fall. Usually for me, a song is something that you finish in one sitting. If it's good enough, you just finish it. It can be a 40-minute sitting or an eight-hour sitting. "Rain King" took 40 minutes. "Mr. Potter's Lullaby" took eight hours. But I would sit there and finish. I would become obsessed and not be able to go do anything else. The last few years, I had not been finishing anything, other than the songs for the play. And when I realized that I wasn't finishing anything, I thought, "Well, I'd better at least not throw them away." Because in the past, if I didn't finish something, I just figured it wasn't good enough and threw it away. But I started keeping everything. I'm usually looking for an atmosphere, a texture….and lean more towards playing an instrument that I can improvise on and play really well…..piano is great…. You can make a "Whirly" (Wurlitzer's early electronic piano) sound magical because it's got a lot of effects on it. But it's kind of more interesting to do that with your hands.…I've been playing a Hammond B3 for a long time, and I know how to do a lot of different things with it. I know how to shape the sound, how to move it somewhere, make it go. My hands know what to do.

It's been around….I like playing accordion because I like the way it makes you feel. I don't play it like an accordion player. I play it like I play it…. I use it as an instrument way more than I would ever use it as a hammer—as a rich, emotional pad, like the way someone might use strings.

So Adam is the writer. All our songs are lyric-driven….All of us, everybody in the band, are musicians in various ways by bringing home chord changes, coming up with new parts, moving things around. There are a few songs of ours that grew almost entirely out of recordings that I made….Then again, the lyrics and melody are all Adam. I think at the end of the day, a song is a lyric and a melody. The chord changes and the instrumental stuff that we do help that melody and the lyrics go.

..there's a learning curve in an instrument… If you're just scrolling through the sounds trying to find something good, you're not going to find something that can play the subtlety…..You can make an instrument sound great by the way you play it, or you can make it sound great by the way you orchestrate it. There are two sides to it.….You could find something to carry a melody, which might be what you want. If you just want to carry a melody, that's fine…..But if you want to shape the song, shape the mood of the song, make it feel like something, you have to play well.

….there's two sides to playing….say you have a Stradivarius violin, you have the best violin in the world. But it's how you play it. It's a big thing. It's just the nature of electronic software instruments that you don't get a lot of practice time. You can't practice some sampler. But there are people who learn certain samplers and synthesizers really well.
It's not what you know. It's how much you practice.
